function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

I’m not able to run shell commands or touch your local machine, but I can walk you through each step and give you the exact files you’ll need to add.  
Below is a quick‑start guide you can copy into your terminal (or paste into a script) after you’ve cloned the repo.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> **Tip** – If you’re using HTTPS instead of SSH, replace the URL with `https://github.com/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git`.

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse & generate artefacts

### 2.1 Dockerfile

Your repo already contains a minimal `Dockerfile`, but let’s make sure it’s production‑ready:

```dockerfile
# Use an official Node runtime as a parent image
FROM node:20-alpine

# Set the working directory inside the container
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Copy package.json and package-lock.json first to leverage Docker cache
COPY package*.json ./

# Install dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy the rest of the source code
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the application
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
```

> **Why this version?**  
> * `node:20-alpine` is lightweight and includes only what you need.  
> * `npm ci --only=production` installs only the production dependencies, keeping the image slim.  
> * `EXPOSE 3000` matches the port used in `app.js`.  

If you prefer to keep the original Dockerfile, just replace its content with the snippet above.

---

### 2.2 Kubernetes YAML

Create a file called `k8s/deployment.yaml` (you can also put it at the repo root if you prefer):

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest   # <-- change to your registry/tag
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
```

> **What this does**  
> * Deploys two replicas of your app.  
> * Exposes them via a LoadBalancer (cloud provider will assign a public IP).  
> * Maps external port 80 → internal port 3000.

Feel free to adjust `replicas`, `image`, or `service_type` to suit your environment.

---

### 2.3 GitHub Actions workflow

Create `.github/workflows/docker-build.yml`:

```yaml
name: Build & Push Docker Image

on:
  push:
    branches: [ main ]

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@v4

    - name: Set up Docker Buildx
      uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

    - name: Log in to GitHub Container Registry
      uses: docker/login-action@v3
      with:
        registry: ghcr.io
        username: ${{ github.actor }}
        password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

    - name: Build and push Docker image
      uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
      with:
        context: .
        file: ./Dockerfile
        push: true
        tags: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:latest
```

> **How it works**  
> * Triggers on pushes to `main`.  
> * Builds the image from the root `Dockerfile`.  
> * Pushes it to GitHub Container Registry under the same name as the repo (`ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome`).  

Make sure you have the `GITHUB_TOKEN` secret available (it’s built‑in).

---

## 3️⃣ Add the new files to Git

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml .github/workflows/docker-build.yml
```

> If you kept the files in the repo root, adjust the paths accordingly.

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, K8s manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

That’s it! Your repo now has a ready‑to‑run Dockerfile, a Kubernetes deployment/service, and a CI pipeline that builds & pushes the image whenever you push to `main`. Happy coding!
